arXiv:1705.05008v1 [math.DG] 14 May 2017

On the asymptotic behavior of the dimension of spaces of harmonic functions with polynomial growth

Xian-Tao Huang Address: School of Mathematics
Sun Yat-sen University
Guangzhou 510275
E-mail address: hxiant@mail2.sysu.edu.cn
Abstract.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, and let hd​(M)h_{d}(M) be the dimension of the space of harmonic functions with polynomial growth of growth order at most dd. Colding and Minicozzi proved that hd​(M)h_{d}(M) is finite. Later on, there are many researches which give better estimates of hd​(M)h_{d}(M). We study the behavior of hd​(M)h_{d}(M) when dd is large in this paper. More precisely, suppose that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has maximal volume growth and has a unique tangent cone at infinity, then when dd is sufficiently large, we obtain some estimates of hd​(M)h_{d}(M) in terms of the growth order dd, the dimension nn and the the asymptotic volume ratio α=limR→∞Vol​(Bp​(R))Rn\alpha=\lim_{R\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathrm{Vol}(B_{p}(R))}{R^{n}}. When α=ωn\alpha=\omega_{n}, i.e., (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is isometric to the Euclidean space, the asymptotic behavior obtained in this paper recovers a well-known asymptotic property of hd​(ℝn)h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 35A01, 53C23, 58J05.

Keywords: Ricci curvature, harmonic function with polynomial growth, eigenvalue.

1. Introduction

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a noncompact complete nn-dimensional manifold. (Throughout this paper, we always assume n≥2n\geq 2.) We fix a point p∈Mp\in M, and denote by ρ⁡(x)=d⁡(x,p)\rho(x)=d(x,p). For a d>0d>0, we consider the linear space:

ℋd(M)={u∈C∞(M)∣Δu=0,u(p)=0,|u(x)|≤K(ρ(x)d+1) for some K}\mathcal{H}_{d}(M)=\{u\in C^{\infty}(M)\mid\Delta u=0,u(p)=0,|u(x)|\leq K(\rho(x)^{d}+1)\text{ for some }K\}

and denote by hd​(M)=dim​ℋd​(M)h_{d}(M)=\textmd{dim}\mathcal{H}_{d}(M).

There are many researches on polynomial growth harmonic functions on manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature.

Yau [48] proved that any positive harmonic function on complete manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature is constant. In [8], Cheng further proved that on such manifolds any harmonic function of sublinear growth must be constant.

On the other hand, it is well-known that hd​(ℝn)∼2(n−1)!​dn−1h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\thicksim\frac{2}{(n-1)!}d^{n-1} as d→∞d\rightarrow\infty.

In view of these results, Yau conjectured that on a manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with non-negative Ricci curvature it always holds hd​(M)<∞h_{d}(M)<\infty.

Li and Tam solved the case for d=1d=1 and the case n=2n=2 of this conjecture (see [39] [40]). Yau’s conjecture was completely solved by Colding and Minicozzi in [12]. Later on, there are many researches which give better estimates of hd​(M)h_{d}(M).

For example, a more precise upper bound for the dimension was obtained:

Theorem 1.1 (see [14], [36]).

If (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature, then there exists a constant C=C⁡(n)>0C=C(n)>0 such that hd​(M)≤C​dn−1h_{d}(M)\leq Cd^{n-1} for all d≥1d\geq 1.

Note that the power n−1n-1 in Theorem 1.1 is sharp compared to the Euclidean case.

The example given by Donnelly (see [20]) shows that we can not expect hd​(Mn)≤hd​(ℝn)h_{d}(M^{n})\leq h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) holds for every dd and every (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with nonnegative Ricci curvature.

On the other hand, in Colding and Minicozzi’s paper [14], they proved that if (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative Ricci curvature then

hd​(M)≤C1​α​dn−1+C2​f​(dn−1),h_{d}(M)\leq C_{1}\alpha d^{n-1}+C_{2}f(d^{n-1}),

where α\alpha is the asymptotic volume ratio; C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are positive constants depending only on nn; the function f:ℝ+→ℝ+f:\mathbb{R}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+} also depends only on nn and satisfies f⁡(t)≤tf(t)\leq t and limt→∞f⁡(t)t=0\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\frac{f(t)}{t}=0. See Theorem 0.26 in [14].

In the case that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has nonnegative sectional curvature, Li and Wang proved that limd→∞d−n​∑i=1dhi−1​(M)≤2​αn!​ωn\lim_{d\rightarrow\infty}d^{-n}\sum_{i=1}^{d}h_{i-1}(M)\leq\frac{2\alpha}{n!\omega_{n}} and lim infd→∞d1−n​hd​(M)≤2​α(n−1)!​ωn\liminf_{d\rightarrow\infty}d^{1-n}h_{d}(M)\leq\frac{2\alpha}{(n-1)!\omega_{n}}, where α\alpha is the asymptotic volume ratio, ωn\omega_{n} is the volume of a unit ball in the nn-dimensional Euclidean space. See Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.3 of [37]. Note that in the case that α=ωn\alpha=\omega_{n}, i.e. (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is isometric to the Euclidean space, the above two inequalities are in fact equalities.

From the theorems in [14] and [37], it seems that the behavior of hd​(M)h_{d}(M) becomes better when dd is large, and the better bound of hd​(M)h_{d}(M) has some relations to the asymptotic volume ratio α\alpha.

In this paper, we also study asymptotic properties of hd​(M)h_{d}(M) when MM has nonnegative Ricci curvature. The following theorem is our main result.

Theorem 1.2.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, i.e. there is a constant α∈(0,ωn]\alpha\in(0,\omega_{n}] such that

α=limr→∞Vol​(Bp​(r))rn.\alpha=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathrm{Vol}(B_{p}(r))}{r^{n}}.

Assume that MM has a unique tangent cone at infinity. Denote by hd=dim​ℋd​(M)h_{d}=\textmd{dim}\mathcal{H}_{d}(M). Then we have

(1.1) limd→∞d−n​∑i=1dhi−1=2​αn!​ωn,\displaystyle\lim_{d\rightarrow\infty}d^{-n}\sum_{i=1}^{d}h_{i-1}=\frac{2\alpha}{n!\omega_{n}},

and

(1.2) lim infd→∞d1−n​hd=2​α(n−1)!​ωn.\displaystyle\liminf_{d\rightarrow\infty}d^{1-n}h_{d}=\frac{2\alpha}{(n-1)!\omega_{n}}.

As a corollary, we have

Corollary 1.3.

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) be a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Suppose that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has maximal volume growth and has a unique tangent cone at infinity, then the following three conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    limd→∞d−n​∑i=1dhi−1=2n!\lim_{d\rightarrow\infty}d^{-n}\sum_{i=1}^{d}h_{i-1}=\frac{2}{n!};

  2. (2)

    limd→∞d1−n​hd=2(n−1)!\lim_{d\rightarrow\infty}d^{1-n}h_{d}=\frac{2}{(n-1)!};

  3. (3)

    (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is isometric to the Euclidean space.

Theorem 1.2 improves the results in Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.3 of [37] in two aspects. Firstly, the assumption that the manifold has nonnegative sectional curvature has been weakened. Secondly, we obtain equalities in (1.1) and (1.2), while in [37], the conclusions are some inequalities.

The proof in [37] considers the level sets of the distance function d⁡(p,⋅)d(p,\cdot). The nonnegative sectional curvature assumption and the smooth structure are used to control some quantities such as the eigenvalues of the level sets and the restriction of harmonic functions on the level sets. In addition, Weyl’s law on smooth manifolds is used in [37].

In the present paper, we combine Li and Wang’s proof ([37]), Cheeger-Colding’s theory (see e.g. [10], [11]) and the recent development in RCD theory to prove Theorem 1.2.

If (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, from Cheeger and Colding’s theory, every tangent cone at infinity of MnM^{n} is a metric cone. However, in general, the tangent cones may be not unique; they depend on the sequences of scales used to blow down the manifold, see [43], [11] for examples. For manifolds with nonnegative sectional curvature, the tangent cone at infinity is unique. There are other sufficient conditions to ensure uniqueness of tangent cone for manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, see e.g. [15].

For a manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, its asymptotically conic property makes the harmonic functions with polynomial growth on it behave like harmonic functions with polynomial growth on a cone. This idea has impact on many works, see [13], [14], [19], [47], [29], [31] etc.

Let’s mention that, in [19], for a manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with nonnegative Ricci curvature, maximal volume growth and unique tangent cone at infinity, it is proved that hd​(M)≥C​dn−1h_{d}(M)\geq Cd^{n-1}, where the constant CC depends on nn and the asymptotic volume ratio. See also [47] and [31] for related researches.

Before we going on introducing the main steps of our proof, let’s give a brief introduction on the study of RCD theory.

Using the theory of optimal transport, Lott, Villani ([41]) and Sturm ([44] [45]) independently introduced the CD​(K,N)\textmd{CD}(K,N)-condition, which is a notion of ‘Ricci bounded from below by K∈ℝK\in\mathbb{R} and dimension bounded above by N∈[1,∞]N\in[1,\infty]’ for general metric measure spaces. Later on, Bacher and Sturm ([7]) introduced reduced curvature-dimension condition CD∗​(K,N)\textmd{CD}^{\ast}(K,N). For N∈[1,∞)N\in[1,\infty), both the CD​(K,N)\textmd{CD}(K,N) condition and CD∗​(K,N)\textmd{CD}^{\ast}(K,N) condition are compatible with the Riemannian case. These two conditions are both stable under the measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence. In particular, measured Gromov-Hausdorff of manifolds with a uniform lower Ricci curvature bound (‘Ricci-limit spaces’ for short) are both CD​(K,N)\textmd{CD}(K,N) spaces and CD∗​(K,N)\textmd{CD}^{\ast}(K,N) spaces. However, both the class of CD​(K,N)\textmd{CD}(K,N) spaces and the class of CD∗​(K,N)\textmd{CD}^{\ast}(K,N) spaces are too large in the sense that they both include Finsler geometries.

Ambrosio, Gigli and Savaré ([6]) introduced the notion of RCD​(K,∞)\textmd{RCD}(K,\infty) spaces (see also [1] for the simplified axiomatization), which rules out Finsler geometries, while retaining the stability properties under measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence. Later on, many researchers began to considered the RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces (for the case of N<∞N<\infty), see [5] [21] [23] etc. To be precise, a RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) space (X,d,m)(X,d,m) is a CD∗​(K,N)\textmd{CD}^{*}(K,N) space such that the Sobolev space W1,2​(X)W^{1,2}(X) is a Hilbert space.

In the recent years there are too many important developments on the RCD∗\textmd{RCD}^{*} theory so that we cannot list them here. Comparing to the properties hold only on manifolds or Ricci-limit spaces, the results obtained on general RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces are ‘intrinsic’ in the sense that their proofs do not depend on the smooth structure. In addition, many recent results on RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces supplement the knowledge on manifolds or Ricci-limit spaces.

On the other hand, there are also many results in Cheeger-Colding’s theory which seem hard to be generalized to general RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces. For example, it is unknown whether the ‘almost volume cone implies almost metric cone’ properties (see [10]) and the structure theory for Gromov-Hausdorff limit of non-collapsed manifolds with a uniform lower Ricci curvature bound (see e.g. [11]) hold on general RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces.

Now we continuous to introduce the main ideas in the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, from the theory in [10] [11], if ri→∞r_{i}\rightarrow\infty, then up to a subsequence, (M,p,gi=ri−2​g)(M,p,g_{i}=r_{i}^{-2}g) convergence in the measured Gromov-Hausdorff sense to some metric measure space (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}) such that (M∞,p∞,ρ∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}) is a metric cone (C⁡(X),p∞,dC⁡(X))(C(X),p_{\infty},d_{C(X)}), and ν∞\nu_{\infty} is a multiple of the Hausdorff measure ℋn\mathcal{H}^{n}.

It is unclear whether the induced metric measure structure on XX, denoted by (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}), is a Ricci-limit space. However, from [33], we know (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) is a RCD∗​(n−2,n−1)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(n-2,n-1) space. This enable us to apply the RCD theory to (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). More precisely, in a recent work [4], Ambrosio, Honda and Tewodrose find a sufficient and necessary condition for Weyl’s law for eigenvalues of Neumann problem on a RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) space. The proof of Weyl’s law in [4] is mainly based on the structure theory of RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces (see [42] [34] [17] [27]) as well as the study of short-time behavior of the heat kernel on RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces. By the structure theory of Cheeger and Colding on C⁡(X)C(X), we know (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) satisfies the criterion in [4], hence Weyl’s law holds on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). See Section 2 for details.

On the other hand, on the conic space (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),ν∞)(C(X),d_{C(X)},\nu_{\infty}), any harmonic function has a very beautiful form, and the eigenfunctions for Neumann problem on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) are closely related to the harmonic functions on C⁡(X)C(X). Furthermore, the sum of roots of eigenvalues for Neumann problem on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) has an interesting property, see Proposition 3.7. These enable us to make use of Weyl’s law on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) to obtain information on harmonic function on C⁡(X)C(X). See Sections 3 and 5 for details.

Thus, in order to finish the proof of Theorem 1.2, the remaining problem is to choose suitable scales to blow down the manifold so that at the same time some information on ℋd​(M)\mathcal{H}_{d}(M) can pass to the limit. This is done in Section 4. We remark that in this step, we use some results on convergence of functions (especially harmonic functions) defined on domain of different spaces. When these spaces are manifolds with a uniform Ricci curvature lower bound, some results are obtained in [18], [46], [28] etc. The more recent researches in [26], [49], [3] etc. show that similar results holds when these spaces are general RCD∗​(K,N)\mathrm{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces.

Combining the arguments from Sections 2 to 5 we can finish the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Finally, we remark that the assumption on the uniqueness of tangent cone at infinity is because of technical reasons. See Remark 5.2 for discussions.

2. Properties of tangent cones at infinity

Following Definition 5.1 in [33], we use the terminology of (0,N)(0,N)-cones throughout this paper :

Definition 2.1 ((0,N)(0,N)-cones).

Suppose (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) is a metric measure space with diam​(X)≤π\textmd{diam}(X)\leq\pi, the (0,N)(0,N)-cone over (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) is a metric measure space (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}) such that:

  • •

    C⁡(X)=X×[0,∞)/(X×{0})C(X)=X\times[0,\infty)/(X\times\{0\});

  • •

    (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)}) is a metric cone with

    dC⁡(X)​((x1,t1),(x2,t2))=t12+t22−2​t1​t2​cos⁡(dX​(x1,x2))d_{C(X)}((x_{1},t_{1}),(x_{2},t_{2}))=\sqrt{t_{1}^{2}+t_{2}^{2}-2t_{1}t_{2}\cos(d_{X}(x_{1},x_{2}))}

    for (x1,t1),(x2,t2)∈C⁡(X)(x_{1},t_{1}),(x_{2},t_{2})\in C(X);

  • •

    mC⁡(X)=tN​d​t⊗mXm_{C(X)}=t^{N}dt\otimes m_{X}.

Obviously, the map Φ:X×(0,∞)→C⁡(X)\Phi:X\times(0,\infty)\rightarrow C(X) is locally bi-Lipschitz. More precisely, given two positive numbers s<rs<r, Φ|X×(r−s,r+s)\Phi|_{X\times(r-s,r+s)} is a (1±Ψ⁡(s,r))(1\pm\Psi(s;r))-bi-Lipschitz map onto its image, here X×(r−s,r+s)X\times(r-s,r+s) is equipped with the product metric, and Ψ⁡(s,r)\Psi(s;r) means a nonnegative function such that when rr is fixed, we have lims→0Ψ⁡(s,r)=0.\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}\Psi(s;r)=0.

For the definition and a quick introduction of properties of RCD∗​(K,N)\mathrm{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces, there are many references, see e.g. Section 2 in [42].

Let (Xi,xi,di,mi)(X_{i},x_{i},d_{i},m_{i}), i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, be a sequence of pointed metric measure spaces, we say (Xi,xi,di,mi)(X_{i},x_{i},d_{i},m_{i}) converges to (X∞,x∞,d∞,m∞)(X_{\infty},x_{\infty},d_{\infty},m_{\infty}) in the pointed measured Gromov-Hausdorff (pmGH for short) sense if there are sequences Ri↑+∞R_{i}\uparrow+\infty, ϵi↓0\epsilon_{i}\downarrow 0 and Borel maps φi:Xi→X∞\varphi_{i}:X_{i}\rightarrow X_{\infty} such that

  1. (1)

    φi​(xi)=x∞\varphi_{i}(x_{i})=x_{\infty};

  2. (2)

    |di​(x,y)−d∞​(φi​(x),φi​(y))|<ϵi|d_{i}(x,y)-d_{\infty}(\varphi_{i}(x),\varphi_{i}(y))|<\epsilon_{i} for any ii and all x,y∈Bxi​(Ri)x,y\in B_{x_{i}}(R_{i});

  3. (3)

    the ϵi\epsilon_{i}-neighbourhood of φi​(Bxi​(Ri))\varphi_{i}(B_{x_{i}}(R_{i})) contains Bx∞​(Ri−ϵi)B_{x_{\infty}}(R_{i}-\epsilon_{i});

  4. (4)

    for any f∈Cb​(X∞)f\in C_{b}(X_{\infty}) with bounded support it holds limn→∞∫f∘φi​d​mi=∫f​d​m∞\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\int f\circ\varphi_{i}dm_{i}=\int fdm_{\infty}.

When all the (Xi,xi,di,mi)(X_{i},x_{i},d_{i},m_{i}) satisfy a uniformly doubling condition, the pmGH convergence is equivalent to the pointed measured Gromov convergence introduced in [26]. See [26] for a detailed study of these notions.

Suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Let ρ\rho be the distance determined by gg, μ\mu be the volume element determined by gg. We can define (Mi,p,ρi,νi)(M_{i},p,\rho_{i},\nu_{i}), where MiM_{i} is the same differential manifold as MnM^{n}, pp is a fixed point on Mi=MnM_{i}=M^{n}, ρi\rho_{i} is the distance determined by the rescaled metric gi=ri−2​gg_{i}=r_{i}^{-2}g, ri→∞r_{i}\rightarrow\infty, and νi\nu_{i} is the renormalized measure defined by

νi​(A):=1μi​(Bp(i)​(1))​μi​(A),\nu_{i}(A):=\frac{1}{\mu_{i}(B^{(i)}_{p}(1))}\mu_{i}(A),

where A⊂MiA\subset M_{i}, and μi\mu_{i} is the volume element determined by gig_{i}. Then by Gromov’s compactness theorem and Theorem 1.6 in [11], up to a subsequence, (Mi,p,ρi,νi)(M_{i},p,\rho_{i},\nu_{i}) converges to some (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}) in the pmGH sense. (M∞,p∞,ρ∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}) is called a tangent cone at infinity of MM. In general, the tangent cones at infinity may not unique.

Suppose in addition (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) has maximal volume growth:

(2.1) α:=limr→∞μ​(Bp​(r))rn>0.\displaystyle\alpha:=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mu(B_{p}(r))}{r^{n}}>0.

From the theory in [10] [11] etc., in this case (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}) has many strong properties.

Firstly, by Theorem 7.6 in [10], (M∞,p∞,ρ∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty}) is a metric cone, i.e. (M∞,p∞,ρ∞)=(C⁡(X),p∞,dC⁡(X))(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty})=(C(X),p_{\infty},d_{C(X)}), where (X,dX)(X,d_{X}) is a compact metric space with diam​(X)≤π\textmd{diam}(X)\leq\pi.

Secondly, by Theorem 5.9 in [11], d​i​mℋ​M∞=ndim_{\mathcal{H}}M_{\infty}=n (in this paper d​i​mℋdim_{\mathcal{H}} means the Hausdorff dimension), and for any R>0R>0 and Mi∋qi→dG​Hz∈M∞M_{i}\ni q_{i}\xrightarrow{d_{GH}}z\in M_{\infty}, we have

(2.2) limi→∞μi​(Bqi(i)​(R))=ℋn​(Bz​(R)).\displaystyle\lim_{i\rightarrow\infty}\mu_{i}(B^{(i)}_{q_{i}}(R))=\mathcal{H}^{n}(B_{z}(R)).

By (2.1) and (2.2) we have

(2.3) ℋn​(Bp∞​(1))=limi→∞μi​(Bp(i)​(1))=limri→∞μ​(Bp​(ri))rin=α,\displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{n}(B_{p_{\infty}}(1))=\lim_{i\rightarrow\infty}\mu_{i}(B^{(i)}_{p}(1))=\lim_{r_{i}\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mu(B_{p}(r_{i}))}{r_{i}^{n}}=\alpha,

and the limit renormalized measure satisfies ν∞=1α​ℋn\nu_{\infty}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathcal{H}^{n}.

Note that d​i​mℋ​X=n−1dim_{\mathcal{H}}X=n-1. Furthermore, ℋn\mathcal{H}^{n} satisfies a co-area formula on C⁡(X)C(X), that is, for any Ω⊂⊂C⁡(X)\Omega\subset\subset C(X),

(2.4) ℋn​(Ω)=∫0∞sn−1​𝑑s​∫Xχ⁡(Ωs)​d​ℋn−1,\displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{n}(\Omega)=\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{n-1}ds\int_{X}\chi(\Omega_{s})d\mathcal{H}^{n-1},

where Ωs={x∈X∣z=(x,s)∈Ω}\Omega_{s}=\{x\in X\mid z=(x,s)\in\Omega\}. See Proposition 7.6 in [29] for a proof. By (2.3) and (2.4), it is easy to see

(2.5) ℋn−1​(X)=n​α.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(X)=n\alpha.

Define the measure mX:=1α​ℋn−1m_{X}:=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathcal{H}^{n-1} on XX, then it is easy to see (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}) is a (0,n−1)(0,n-1)-cone over (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}).

In the next, we use the RCD theory to study (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)=(C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty})=(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}) and (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}).

Obviously, (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty}) is an RCD∗​(0,n)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(0,n) space. Thus by Corollary 1.3 of [33], we further know that the cross section (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) is an RCD∗​(n−2,n−1)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(n-2,n-1) space. In particular, we know (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) satisfies a volume doubling property and Poincaré inequality (in fact, to derive these two properties on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}), we can also use the arguments in [18] to avoid the use of the RCD property).

Let ΔX\Delta_{X} be the Laplacian operator on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Let 0=λ0<λ1≤λ2≤…0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots be the eigenvalues of ΔX\Delta_{X}, {φi​(x)}i=0∞\{\varphi_{i}(x)\}_{i=0}^{\infty} be the corresponding eigenfunctions, i.e.

(2.6) −ΔX​φi​(x)=λi​φi​(x).\displaystyle-\Delta_{X}\varphi_{i}(x)=\lambda_{i}\varphi_{i}(x).

We require ∫X|φi|2​d​mX=1\int_{X}|\varphi_{i}|^{2}dm_{X}=1, and ∫Xφi​φj​d​mX=0\int_{X}\varphi_{i}\varphi_{j}dm_{X}=0 for every i≠ji\neq j. Note that λi→∞\lambda_{i}\rightarrow\infty and {φi​(x)}i=0∞\{\varphi_{i}(x)\}_{i=0}^{\infty} spans L2​(X,mX)L^{2}(X,m_{X}), which can be derived from a standard argument basing on a Rellich-type Compactness Theorem. Every φi\varphi_{i} always has a Lipschitz representative in the corresponding Sobolev class (see [32]). In the remaining part of this paper, the φi\varphi_{i}’s are always required to be Lipschitz.

Recently, Weyl’s law on RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces has been studied. In [4], Ambrosio, Honda and Tewodrose gives a sufficient and necessary condition for the Weyl’s law for eigenvalues of Neumann problem on compact RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces, see Theorem 4.3 in [4]. (See [49] for Weyl’s law for eigenvalues of Dirichlet problem on RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) spaces.) Before we give a statement of Weyl’s law, we first introduce some notion and background knowledge.

Definition 2.2.

The kk-dimensional regular set ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k} of an RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) space (X,d,m)(X,d,m) is the set of points x∈supp​mx\in\mathrm{supp}m such that

(X,r−1​d,1m​(Bx​(r))​m,x)→p​m​G​H(ℝk,dℝk,1ωk​ℋk,0k)(X,r^{-1}d,\frac{1}{m(B_{x}(r))}m,x)\xrightarrow{pmGH}(\mathbb{R}^{k},d_{\mathbb{R}^{k}},\frac{1}{\omega_{k}}\mathcal{H}^{k},0_{k})

as r→0+r\rightarrow 0^{+}.

We remark that the definition of the regular set in Definition 2.2 is a bit different from that of Mondino and Naber (see [42]). However, the two definitions are equivalent, see Remark 3.5 in [4]. Thus, by [42], the following structure theorem holds.

Theorem 2.3 (see [42]).

Let (X,d,m)(X,d,m) be an RCD∗​(K,N)\mathrm{RCD}^{*}(K,N) space with K∈ℝK\in\mathbb{R} and N∈(1,∞)N\in(1,\infty). Then

m⁡(X∖⋃k=1[N]ℛk)=0.m(X\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^{[N]}\mathcal{R}_{k})=0.

Moreover, for any sufficiently small ϵ\epsilon, we can cover each ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k}, up to an mm-negligible subset, by a countable collection of sets {Uϵk,l}l\{U_{\epsilon}^{k,l}\}_{l} such that each Uϵk,lU_{\epsilon}^{k,l} is (1+ϵ)(1+\epsilon)-biLipschitz to a subset of ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}.

As in [4], we have the following definitions.

Definition 2.4.

Suppose (X,d,m)(X,d,m) is an RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) space. dimd,m​(X)\mathrm{dim}_{d,m}(X) is defined to be the largest integer kk such that ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k} has positive mm-measure. For any positive integer kk, ℛk∗⊂ℛk\mathcal{R}^{*}_{k}\subset\mathcal{R}_{k} is defined to be

ℛk∗:={x∈ℛk|∃limr→0+m​(Bx​(r))ωk​rk∈(0,∞)}.\mathcal{R}^{*}_{k}:=\bigl\{x\in\mathcal{R}_{k}\bigl|\exists\lim_{r\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{m(B_{x}(r))}{\omega_{k}r^{k}}\in(0,\infty)\bigr\}.

On a compact RCD∗​(K,N)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(K,N) space (X,d,m)(X,d,m), we consider the Neumann eigenvalue problems, and let 0=λ0<λ1≤λ2≤…0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots be the eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Let

N(X,d,m)​(λ):=#⁡{i∈ℕ+|λi≤λ}\displaystyle N_{(X,d,m)}(\lambda):=\#\{i\in\mathbb{N}^{+}|\lambda_{i}\leq\lambda\}

be the counting function.

The following theorem is a special case of Weyl’s law obtained from [4]:

Theorem 2.5 (see Corollary 4.4 in [4]).

Let (X,d,m)(X,d,m) be a compact RCD∗​(K,N)\mathrm{RCD}^{*}(K,N) space with K∈ℝK\in\mathbb{R} and N∈(1,∞)N\in(1,\infty), and let k=dimd,m​Xk=\mathrm{dim}_{d,m}X. Suppose k=Nk=N, then we have

(2.7) limλ→∞N(X,d,m)​(λ)λk2=ωk(2​π)k​ℋk​(ℛk∗)<∞.\displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow\infty}\frac{N_{(X,d,m)}(\lambda)}{\lambda^{\frac{k}{2}}}=\frac{\omega_{k}}{(2\pi)^{k}}\mathcal{H}^{k}(\mathcal{R}^{*}_{k})<\infty.

In the following, we will apply Theorem 2.5 to the RCD∗​(n−2,n−1)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(n-2,n-1) space (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}), where XX is the cross section of a tangent cone at infinity of (M,g)(M,g) as in the beginning of this section. In view of Weyl’s law in the form of (2.7), the most important point is to understand k=dimdX,mX​Xk=\mathrm{dim}_{d_{X},m_{X}}X and ℛk∗\mathcal{R}^{*}_{k}.

We will apply the structure theory of Cheeger and Colding on the Ricci-limit space (M∞,p∞,ρ∞,ν∞)=(C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(M_{\infty},p_{\infty},\rho_{\infty},\nu_{\infty})=(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}) to get information on the structure of (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}).

Recall that in Definition 0.1 of [11], a point y∈C⁡(X)y\in C(X) is called kk-regular if every tangent cone at yy is isometric to ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}. Let ℛ~k\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{k} be the set of kk-regular points on C⁡(X)C(X). Here we note that even though in the definition of [11], at a kk-regular points, the limit measure on ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} is not stated, but from the arguments in Proposition 1.35 of [11], we can easily prove that the limit measure on the tangent cone ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} is just a multiple of the standard Hausdorff measure. Thus when restricted to the Ricci-limit spaces, the kk-regular points in the sense of [42] (see Definition 2.2) coincides with the ones in [11].

Proposition 2.6.

Suppose (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}) is a tangent cone at infinity of a manifold (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) with nonnegative Ricci curvature satisfying (2.1). 3. Harmonic functions on cones

We study harmonic functions on cones in this section. Even though what we need in this paper are results on cone-liked Ricci-limit spaces, we obtain results in the general setting of RCD\mathrm{RCD} spaces here. More precisely, in this section we consider the following setting. Suppose (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}) is a RCD∗​(n−2,n−1)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(n-2,n-1) space, (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}) is a (0,n−1)(0,n-1)-cone over (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}), hence a RCD∗​(0,n)\textmd{RCD}^{*}(0,n) space. Denote by p∞p_{\infty} the vertex of C⁡(X)C(X), and by Bp∞​(R)B_{p_{\infty}}(R) the open geodesic balls of radius RR centred at p∞p_{\infty}. Let ΔX\Delta_{X} be the Laplacian operator on (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Let 0=λ0<λ1≤λ2≤…0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots be the Neumann eigenvalues of ΔX\Delta_{X}, {φi​(x)}i=0∞\{\varphi_{i}(x)\}_{i=0}^{\infty} be the corresponding eigenfunctions, i.e.

for any Lipschitz function vv with supp⁡(v)⊂⊂U\mathrm{supp}(v)\subset\subset U. In [19], it is proved that suppose (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth, and suppose that MM has a unique tangent cone at infinity, then hd​(M)≥C​dn−1h_{d}(M)\geq Cd^{n-1} for some constant CC depending on nn and α\alpha; see Theorem 0.1 of [19]. During the proof of [19], the author in fact obtain the following more stronger result (see also Theorem 1.2 of [31] for a more general result which may hold in some collapsed cases):

Theorem 5.1 (See [19] and [31]).

Assume that (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and satisfies (2.1). Assume that MM has a unique tangent cone at infinity, which is denoted by (C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X))(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}). Let 0=λ0<λ1≤λ2≤…0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots be the Neumann eigenvalues on the cross section (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Let N(X,dX,mX)N_{(X,d_{X},m_{X})} be the counting function. Then given any d>0d>0 such that d⁡(d+n−2)>λ1d(d+n-2)>\lambda_{1}, we have

(5.1) hd≥N(X,dX,mX)​(d⁡(d+n−2)−ϵ)−1\displaystyle h_{d}\geq N_{(X,d_{X},m_{X})}(d(d+n-2)-\epsilon)-1

for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

We will complete the proof of Theorem 1.2 in this section. In the proof, we always assume dd is sufficiently large. Since k=hd​A−1Ak=h_{d}\frac{A-1}{A}, kk is a large number. Furthermore, note that

hence ss is also a large number.

Proof of Corollary 1.3.

It is well known that (1) and (2) hold on Euclidean space, see Appendix B in [35] for a detailed proof. On the other hand, if (1) or (2) holds, then from (1.1), (1.2) and the volume comparison theorem, (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) must be isometric to the Euclidean space. ∎

Remark 5.2.

We remark that, in the proof of Theorem 1.2, the i0i_{0} (such that (5.4) holds for any i≥i0i\geq i_{0}) depends on ξ\xi and the cross section XX. On the other hand, if we do not assume the tangent cone at infinity is unique, the tangent cone at infinity C⁡(X)C(X) depends on dd and other parameters used to blow down the manifold, thus in this case we cannot obtain (5.12) directly by letting d→∞d\rightarrow\infty. This is one of the reasons why in Theorem 1.2 we assume the tangent cone at infinity is unique. The other reason is that we use Theorem 5.1, whose proof also make use of the uniqueness of the tangent cone at infinity. In fact, it is an open question whether there exists a nontrivial polynomial growth harmonic function on a manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and maximal volume growth. It is also an interesting question whether the conclusion in Theorem 1.2 holds without the assumption on uniqueness of tangent cone at infinity.
